title: Preparation of Di-benzal acetone
objective: Carry out the reaction under the specified conditions
Isolate the crude solid product by filtration/precipitation
Determine the melting point of the purified product as a purity check, and calculate the percentage yield

theory.statement: Benzaldehyde and acetone undergo a base-catalysed aldol condensation (Claisen-Schmidt reaction): acetone's enolate attacks two equivalents of benzaldehyde in succession, and each aldol product dehydrates to give the doubly-conjugated, yellow crystalline dibenzalacetone.
theory.derivationNote: Crude yield is always higher than the yield after recrystallisation — the gap between the two is a direct, quantitative measure of the impurity removed in one recrystallisation. The melting point of the purified solid, sharp and close to the literature value, is the check that the removed material really was impurity and not product.

apparatus.name: Benzaldehyde
apparatus.why: The aldehyde condensing twice with acetone

apparatus.name: Sodium hydroxide solution
apparatus.why: Base catalyst for the aldol condensation and dehydration

procedure.text: Set up the reaction with the specified reagents, cooling as required for this exothermic step.
Once the reaction is complete, isolate the crude solid by filtration (or by pouring onto crushed ice, as appropriate).
Weigh the crude product and calculate the crude percentage yield.
Recrystallise from a suitable solvent, filter, and dry the purified crystals.
Determine the melting point of the purified product and compare with the literature value.

steps: Isolate and weigh the crude product; crude % yield
Determine the melting point as a purity check

expectedResult.quantity: Melting point of the purified product
expectedResult.statement: The crude product is obtained in good yield; recrystallisation lowers the yield but sharpens the melting point towards the literature value of about 112.0 °C, confirming the gain in purity.

safety: Benzaldehyde has a strong, penetrating odour — use in a ventilated area.
Sodium hydroxide solution is corrosive — avoid skin/eye contact.
sourcesOfError: Too little base or too short a reaction time gives incomplete condensation (mono-benzalacetone contamination).
Poor temperature control affects the ratio of mono- to di-condensation product.
Impure benzaldehyde (containing benzoic acid from air-oxidation) lowers the yield.

viva.question: Why are two equivalents of benzaldehyde used per equivalent of acetone?
viva.expectedConcept: Acetone has two sets of alpha-hydrogens (on both sides of the carbonyl), so under base catalysis it can condense with benzaldehyde at both positions in succession, giving the doubly-condensed, conjugated dibenzalacetone rather than stopping at a single aldol product.
viva.answerLogic: Symmetric double condensation at both alpha-carbons.
viva.commonMisconception: Expecting only a single condensation (benzalacetone) under these conditions.

viva.question: Why is dibenzalacetone yellow, while benzaldehyde and acetone are both colourless?
viva.expectedConcept: The product has an extended, conjugated system of alternating double bonds (two C=C plus the C=O) spanning both phenyl rings, which shifts its light absorption into the visible region, giving it colour that neither simple starting material has.
viva.answerLogic: Extended conjugation lowers the HOMO-LUMO gap into the visible range.
viva.commonMisconception: Attributing the colour to an impurity rather than to the product's own conjugated structure.

preLab.question: Recrystallisation is expected to:
options: Lower the yield but increase the purity
Increase the yield but lower the purity
Change the product into a different compound
preLab.feedback: Some product is always lost in the mother liquor during recrystallisation, but what remains is purer, shown by a sharper, higher melting point.

duringLab.question: Complete the preparation and record both crude and purified yield.

postLab.question: State the melting point of the purified product (°C).

scientificValidation.formula: % yield = (obtained/theoretical) × 100; melting point as purity check
assumptions: Reaction goes to a realistic, not complete, conversion
One recrystallisation removes most but not all impurity
edgeCases: Poor cooling during an exothermic step lowers both yield and purity
expectedBehaviour: Purified yield < crude yield; purified m.p. closer to literature value
